chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad al-Halabi, who said:

I asked Aba 'Abd Allah عليه السلام about a man who struck another man's head with a pickaxe, so that his eyes flowed down onto his cheeks. Then the one who had been struck sprang upon his assailant and killed him. He said:

So Abu 'Abd Allah عليه السلام said: “These two are both transgressors. I do not hold that there is qawad against the one who killed the man, because he killed him at the time he killed him while he was blind, and the offense of a blind person is treated as a mistake; his 'aqilah is liable for it, and they are charged with it over three years, one installment in each year. If the blind man has no 'aqilah, then the diyah of what he committed is binding upon him from his own property, to be taken from it over three years. And the blind man may recourse against the heirs of his assailant for the diyah of his two eyes.”

key_terms.أَعْمَى: blind; the legal status affecting liability in this case
key_terms.جِنَايَتُهُ: his offense or injurious act, considered in legal liability
key_terms.خَطَأٌ: mistaken or non-deliberate in legal classification
key_terms.دِيَةُ: financial compensation due for injury or killing
key_terms.عَاقِلَتَهُ: his paternal kin group legally responsible for paying diyah in certain cases
key_terms.قَوَدًا: retaliatory execution or legal retaliation for killing
key_terms.مِعْوَلٍ: a pickaxe or mattock used as the striking instrument
key_terms.وَرَثَةِ: the heirs from whom compensation may be claimed

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man is blinded in an assault and then kills his attacker?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning reciprocal injury, homicide, and liability when blindness results from an assault. Imam al-Sadiq عليه السلام rules that no retaliatory execution applies here, because the killer had become blind at the moment of the killing, and the liability for his act is treated as mistaken offense with diyah distributed over three years. The narration also establishes the blind victim’s right to claim compensation for the loss of his eyes from the heirs of the original assailant.
